title: Faster (\Delta + 1)-Edge Coloring: Breaking the m \sqrt{n} Time Barrier
authors: Sayan Bhattacharya (Warwick University, United Kingdom), Din Carmon (Tel Aviv University, Israel), Martin Costa (Warwick University, United Kingdom), Shay Solomon (Tel Aviv University, Israel), Tianyi Zhang (Tel Aviv University, Israel)
abstract: Vizing's theorem states that any $n$-vertex $m$-edge graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ can be {\em edge colored} using at most $\Delta + 1$ different colors [Diskret.~Analiz, '64]. Vizing's original proof is algorithmic and shows that such an edge coloring can be found in $\tilde{O}(mn)$ time. This was subsequently improved to $\tilde O(m\sqrt{n})$, independently by Arjomandi [1982] and by Gabow et al.~[1985]. In this paper we present an algorithm that computes such an edge coloring in $\tilde O(mn^{1/3})$ time, giving the first polynomial improvement for this fundamental problem in over 40 years.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Consider a simple, undirected graph G = (V, E) with
maximum degree ∆, and an integer κ ∈ N+ . A κ-edge
coloring ψ : E → {1, 2, . . . , κ} of G assigns a “color” ψ(e)
to every edge e ∈ E, in such a way that no two adjacent edges
receive the same color. What is the minimum κ for which G
admits a κ-edge coloring? This value is known as the “edge
chromatic number” of G. Any edge coloring trivially requires
at least ∆ colors. On the other hand, a textbook theorem
by Vizing guarantees that at most ∆ + 1 colors are always
sufficient [1], and it is NP-complete to distinguish whether the
edge chromatic number of a given graph is ∆ or ∆+1 [2]. This
leads naturally to a fundamental question in graph algorithms,
summarized below.

A. Related Work
√
If we allow for a larger palette of ∆ + Õ( ∆) colors, then
the problem can be solved in Õ(m) time [6]. In addition, there
exist algorithms which achieve linear or near-linear runtime for
(1 + ϵ)∆-edge coloring [7]–[9].
Quite a few improved results have been obtained over the
years for restricted graph classes. For bipartite graphs one
can always compute a ∆-edge coloring in Õ(m) time [10].
For bounded degree graphs one can compute a (∆ + 1)edge coloring in Õ(m∆) time [4], a classic result that was
generalized recently for bounded arboricity graphs [11]; see
[12]–[14] for further recent works on edge coloring in bounded
arboricity graphs. Subfamilies of bounded arboricity graphs,
in particular planar graphs, bounded treewidth graphs and
bounded genus graphs, were studied in [15]–[17].
Finally, in recent years substantive effort has been devoted to
the study of the edge coloring problem in other computational
models; such as dynamic algorithms [7], [8], [18]–[21], online
algorithms [22]–[26], distributed algorithms [20], [27]–[34],
and streaming algorithms [35]–[38].

How fast can we compute a (∆ + 1)-edge coloring of
an input graph with n vertices and m edges?

Finally, let us finish our main theorem. By Theorem IV.1,
the main theorem holds whenever ∆ ≤ n2/3 , so we are left
with the case that ∆ > n2/3 .
The algorithm is by a recursive application of Eulerian
partition provided by Lemma III.2. Basically, on input tuple
(G0 = (V, E0 ), ∆0 ), if ∆0 ≤ n2/3 , then simply run the
algorithm from Theorem IV.1 to find a (∆0 +1)-edge coloring
in time Õ(mn1/3 ). Otherwise, apply Lemma III.2 on G0 ,
which produces a partition G0 = G1 ∪ G2 in linear time
O(|E0 |) into two subgraphs G1 and G2 with maximum
degrees ⌊∆0 /2⌋ ≤ ∆1 , ∆2 ≤ ⌈∆0 /2⌉, respectively. After that,
recursively compute two edge colorings with disjoint color
palettes ψ1 , ψ2 on tuples (G1 , ∆1 ) and (G2 , ∆2 ) respectively.
Since ψ1 , ψ2 are using disjoint color palettes, the total
number of different colors in ψ1 , ψ2 is at most ∆0 + 3. To
remove the extra colors, pick the two least popular colors
under ψ1 , ψ2 and uncolor all the edges with these two colors.
Now let ψ be the union of ψ1 , ψ2 , which is now a partial
coloring of E0 with at most 2|E0 |/∆0 uncolored edges. Then,
apply the standard Vizing’s procedure to extend ψ to these
edges, which takes total time Õ(|E0 |n/∆0 ) = Õ(|E0 |n1/3 ),
which concludes the proof.
